NO obituary found; the oral-history project implies she was alive at interview, but no recent confirmation, so alive=unknown. After her 2016 retirement the dedicated metals/jewelry teaching was not continued — current Studio Art concentrations are Ceramics, Painting, and Sculpture, with no metals/jewelry courses or specialist faculty. Sadler was named professor emeritus and died March 12, 2023, at age 74. programs.name: New Mexico State University — Jewelry and Metalsmithing (Department of Art)
programs.current_name: Jewelry and Metalsmithing area, Department of Art, New Mexico State University
programs.current_status: Active. Jewelry/metalsmithing is one of the studio specialization areas within the NMSU Department of Art (College of Arts & Sciences), Las Cruces. Students can specialize in jewelry/metalsmithing through the BFA in Studio Art and the MFA in Studio Art (a 60-credit, 3-year terminal degree). The department also offers a BA in Art and an MA in Art History. The metals studio is housed in Devasthali Hall (Rm 118), a newer facility with 16 benches, casting/forming rooms, an outdoor courtyard with lapidary/powder-coating, and digital tools (3D printing with castable wax, laser cutting).
programs.current_chair: Metals/jewelry area led by Motoko Furuhashi (Associate Professor of Jewelry & Metalsmithing; MFA in Metals, Univ. of Illinois Urbana-Champaign). She heads the area, not the full Department of Art; the overall department chair was not confirmed in this check.
programs.what_happened: Continuation with a generational faculty turnover. The archived directory's listed faculty (Carlyle Smith guest 1962–79, Patrice Case, Kate Wagle 1982–88, Lisa Norton 1989–92, "Julia Barrelo 1992–present") no longer reflects current staffing — the named "to present" faculty member is not the current lead. Since ~2014 the program has been led in jewelry/metalsmithing by Motoko Furuhashi (an "Artist in Residence in Metals and Jewelry" posting appears on the department site dated June 2014). The program moved into the new Devasthali Hall art building (opened ~2020) with an upgraded metals studio. It runs a long-standing student Annual Jewelry Sale (42nd+ annual in recent years) and remains active through 2025. No closure, merger, or rename — the area persists within the Department of Art.
programs.notes: Program is unambiguously still operating. The discrepancy is in the FACULTY record, not program existence: none of the archived faculty names (Carlyle Smith, Patrice Case, Kate Wagle, Lisa Norton, Julia/Julia Barrelo) appear on the current NMSU site; current lead is Motoko Furuhashi. "Metals program started: unknown" remains unverified — not established in this check. Department chair of Art (vs. metals area head) not separately confirmed. Jewelry/metalsmithing is an emphasis area, not a standalone named degree, so degrees are the BFA Studio Art / MFA Studio Art with metals specialization.

Courses still offered include ART-UE 501 Metalsmithing I for Non-Majors (listed for Spring 2026) and ART-UE 1515 Metalsmithing (sculpture/small-metal construction). It continues as such through 2025-2026 with active course offerings, so there has been continuation rather than closure or rename. The archived faculty name "Pamela E. Lins 1989 to present" almost certainly refers to artist/sculptor Pam Lins, who is no longer at NYU; she now teaches at Cooper Union (adjunct), Princeton University (Lewis Center for the Arts), and Bard College MFA. Departmental leadership over the period is held by chair Nancy Deihl.
programs.notes: Important caveat: the archived directory listed NYU as a 'metals program,' but at NYU metalsmithing/jewelry is a concentration/medium inside the broader Studio Art BFA/MFA, not a dedicated metals or CAD-CAM jewelry degree. So it 'still exists' in the sense that metalsmithing teaching continues, but there is no standalone metals program to close or rename. Pam Lins's departure from NYU could not be precisely dated from public sources; her current affiliations (Cooper Union, Princeton, Bard) are confirmed via Wikipedia and institutional bios. Could not confirm the specific instructor currently leading metalsmithing sections. Course code 'ARTUE 501' (per Coursicle) corresponds to NYU's ART-UE prefix for undergraduate Studio Art.

programs.notes: North Bennet Street School is a private vocational/trade school in Boston's North End, accredited as a non-degree-granting institution, so its programs award diplomas rather than academic degrees (AA/BA/BFA). Previous department head before Darji (Sept 2023) not explicitly named in sources, though Rosemary Trainor JM '90 was a longtime instructor.

No evidence the metals program was merged or renamed into a surviving track; it simply lapsed.

James Malenda (the 1976–1987 faculty member) went on to Kutztown University as Professor of Fine Metals from 1987, consistent with his Bradley tenure ending in 1987. programs.what_happened: The institution archived as "Oregon School of Arts & Crafts" (the name used 1978–1996) was renamed "Oregon College of Art and Craft" (OCAC) in 1996. OCAC began granting the BFA in 1994 and added an MFA in Craft by fall 2013. Facing severe financial difficulty, OCAC explored mergers in late 2018 / early 2019 with Pacific Northwest College of Art (PNCA) and then Portland State University; both fell through. The board voted to close, and OCAC held its final commencement on May 19, 2019, ending 112 years of operation. The renowned metalsmithing program — notably the only US program still requiring a functional hollowware teapot — closed along with the school. Christine Clark, who led the Metals department, had relinquished the chair role by 2018–2019 and continued teaching part-time through the closure.
programs.notes: "Oregon School of Arts & Crafts" and "Oregon College of Art and Craft" are the same institution (renamed 1996), NOT a merger of two schools. Do not confuse with separate, still-operating programs: University of Oregon (ARTM Metalsmithing & Jewelry) and Pacific Northwest College of Art (PNCA, which absorbed OCAC's MFA in Applied Craft + Design partnership before OCAC's full closure). OCAC's archives went to the Oregon Historical Society / Archives West. The directory link slug points to an internal archived page; the canonical surviving reference is the Wikipedia article since ocac.edu is defunct.

Closure date is firmly documented as December 15, 2017. The school was NOT renamed or merged; it simply ceased operation when the founder retired and no buyer materialized. The closest "continuation" of Alan Revere's teaching is (a) his online community "Let's Make Professional Jewelry" and (b) his consulting work on GIA's Graduate Jeweler program in Carlsbad — but neither is the Revere Academy. Best canonical link is the founder's own retrospective page (the original revereacademy.com site is offline). Confidence high; multiple independent trade sources plus the founder's own site agree.

programs.current_status: BFA in Jewelry & Metal Arts, within the Fine Arts Division (now organized under an "Interdisciplinary 3D Fine Arts" cluster). programs.what_happened: The institution was renamed: California College of Arts and Crafts (CCAC) became California College of the Arts (CCA) in 2003. The Jewelry/Metal Arts program (founded 1912; the program celebrated "100 years" c. 2012) continued strongly past 2014. Marilyn da Silva, who was the program/department head (since 1987) and is listed in the archived record as "? to present," has since retired to Professor Emeritus status. Leadership moved to a co-chair / interdisciplinary-cluster structure (interim co-chairs Aaron Gach and Katherine Lam), with Curtis Arima now Dean of Fine Arts. The biggest change: on January 13, 2026, CCA announced it will wind down and close by the end of the 2026-2027 academic year under an agreement in which Vanderbilt University acquires the campus and will establish its own art/design programming for 2027-28. Students on track to graduate by end of 2026-27 finish at CCA; transfer/teach-out pathways are being arranged for others. So the metals program still operates now but is on a defined teach-out toward institutional closure.
programs.notes: Archived faculty maps to the well-documented CCAC/CCA program lineage: Bob Winston (1942-1956), Martin Streich, Marilyn da Silva (now Emeritus), Dawn Nakanishi (adjunct). The institution is the same one, post-rename (CCAC to CCA, 2003). Current degree is BFA (no standalone Jewelry/Metal Arts MFA found on the program page; MFA at CCA is in Fine Arts more broadly). Co-chairs are noted as "interim," indicating a transitional leadership state amid the wind-down. Watch the Vanderbilt transition: after 2026-27 the CCA degree ceases; Vanderbilt's future SF art/design offerings are a separate institution, not a continuation of this specific program.

programs.name: The University of the Arts
programs.current_name: The University of the Arts (closed)
programs.current_status: Closed. No degrees offered. The entire university ceased operations June 7, 2024; the metals/jewelry program (in the School of Art's Crafts area) closed with it.
programs.current_chair: None (institution dissolved). Last university president was Kerry Walk.
programs.what_happened: The University of the Arts in Philadelphia abruptly announced closure on May 31, 2024, ceasing operations June 7, 2024. The Middle States Commission on Higher Education withdrew its accreditation effective June 1, 2024. The university filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy liquidation on September 13, 2024. The institution and all of its programs, including the historic crafts/metals/jewelry program, were permanently closed. Displaced students transferred to nearby schools including Temple University (Tyler School of Art), Moore College of Art & Design, and Drexel.
programs.notes: The metals/jewelry program descends from the historic Philadelphia College of Art (PCA) / Philadelphia Museum School craft lineage; the archived faculty list (Nacke, Yellin, Gilchrist, Cute, Reinhardt, Skoogfors) matches that pedigree — Skoogfors chaired the Craft Department in the late 1960s and Reinhardt led the metal/jewelry area and later became dean of visual arts as PCA became UArts. The program sat in the School of Art's Crafts area before closure. No surviving successor program exists at UArts; the closest active metals/jewelry/CAD-CAM program in Philadelphia is the unrelated one at Temple University's Tyler School of Art & Architecture (which absorbed some displaced students but is a separate institution and program). Note: the historic UArts metals program was NOT itself a CAD-CAM program; the CAD-CAM emphasis belongs to Temple/Tyler.

programs.current_name: Department of Art and Art History (College of Liberal Arts)
programs.current_status: No standalone metals/jewelry/metalsmithing concentration remains. The Department of Art and Art History offers BA in Art, BA in Art History, BFA in Art, and an MFA. Current studio concentrations are Art Education, Cinematic Arts, Clay, Drawing, Glass, Painting, Photography, Printmaking, Sculpture, and Visual Communication Design. "Metals" survives only as a medium mentioned within the broader 3D/sculpture studio offerings, not as a named program.
programs.current_chair: Dr. August Jordan Davis (Chair, Department of Art and Art History, as of 2025)
programs.what_happened: David Keens introduced the Metals-Jewelry Program at UTA in 1973 and was its founding figure (the archived "1974 to present" entry corresponds to his career). Over time Keens's work and the program's emphasis shifted into glass; he built and coordinated UTA's nationally recognized Glass Program. Keens retired in 2013 after 39 years on the faculty. The original Metals-Jewelry Program did not survive as a distinct, named area: by the current era the department lists Glass and Sculpture (plus Clay, etc.) as its 3D concentrations, with metals referenced only as one medium within 3D/sculpture study. So since ~2014 the metals/jewelry identity has effectively been absorbed/superseded — primarily by the Glass program Keens founded out of it — rather than continued under its own name. Department leadership has since passed to Chair August Jordan Davis (2025).
programs.notes: The archived record's "David Keens 1974 to present" reflects the founding-faculty era. Best read: program merged/renamed rather than cleanly closed. Keens started the Metals-Jewelry program (dept history page dates it to 1973) but became internationally known for glass and was named Texas State Artist in 3D Media (2007); he retired 2013. No current UTA page advertises a metals or jewelry concentration; glass and sculpture are the live 3D areas. Could not find an explicit statement "metals program closed" — inference is from absence in current concentration lists plus Keens's documented pivot to glass and retirement. Chair identification (Davis) is from a 2025 search snippet, not directly re-verified on the department page.

By the ~2014-present period the discipline survives only as metal-fabrication facilities and occasional coursework folded into the 3D4M (ceramics + glass + sculpture) area; there is no metals/jewelry degree track. The Seattle Metals Guild absorbed some of the community/education role the program had filled. The 3D4M program itself is active (e.g., 2024 Open House); Mary Lee Hu received the 2024 SNAG Lifetime Achievement Award.
programs.notes: Archived faculty roster matches the historic UW metals program (Ruth Pennington founding-era, John Marshall, Mary Lee Hu, Lynne Hull). The current art.washington.edu domain still lists "Metal Art" as a field-of-interest tag, but that does not correspond to an active standalone degree. No current program-head specific to metals could be confirmed. programs.name: University of Wisconsin-Madison
programs.current_name: Art Metals / Metalsmithing and Jewelry area, Art Department, University of Wisconsin-Madison
programs.current_status: Active and thriving. Sits within the Art Department (School of Education), as part of the Contemporary 3D Practices disciplines. Offers BS/BFA-level study (undergrad Art major with metals concentration) and a 3-year MFA in Art with a metalsmithing/art-metals focus. Course sequence runs Art 244 Art Metal I through Art 644 Advanced Art Metal II plus special topics (enameling, holloware, pewtersmithing). Program is ranked No. 3 nationally for metals/jewelry; department is top-15 in fine arts (US News).
programs.current_chair: Lisa Gralnick is the long-tenured Professor of Art Metal (at UW-Madison since 2001/2007; previously head of Jewelry & Metals at Parsons 1991-2001). The department added a new tenure-track Assistant Professor of Art Metals via a 2024-25 search. Art Department chair is a separate rotating role (Tom Loeser, CR Skip Johnson Professor, chaired 2009-2014).
programs.what_happened: Strong continuation since ~2014. The program descends directly from the historic faculty in the archived record (Vierthaler, Fenster, Moty, Hu, Glowacki) and remains one of the oldest, most respected metals/jewelry programs in the US. Lisa Gralnick has carried the professorship through this period. In September 2024 the department launched a search for a new tenure-track Assistant Professor of Art Metals (apps due Nov 7, 2024), indicating active investment and faculty renewal/expansion rather than any decline. The metals labs remain fully equipped (casting, enameling, forging, machining) with a full-time technician. No closure, merger, or rename.
programs.notes: The archived directory page (s246.html) listed historic mid-century faculty (Arthur Vierthaler 1946-1976, Fred Fenster 1962-, Eleanor Moty 1972-2000, Mary Lee Hu 1976-77, Martha Glowacki) — these are foundational figures of the program's lineage, all now departed. Current public-facing identity is the "Metalsmithing and Jewelry" / "Art Metals" area within the Art Department. The art.wisc.edu/areas/art-metals/ path resolves but currently surfaces an event page rather than a stable area-overview page; the department homepage and the guide.wisc.edu MFA/course pages are the most stable canonical references. Some sources sit under education.wisc.edu because the Art Department is housed in the School of Education.

Madden, 1992 to present" from the archived record). Earlier chairs of the Crafts/Craft & Material Studies dept included Madden (through ~2014) and glass artist Kim Harty (~2020).

In August 2023, CCS combined the former Art Practice and Craft and Material Studies majors into one reenvisioned "Studio Art & Craft" BFA (chair Valerie Jenkins). Metalsmithing/Jewelry survived every reorganization as a named discipline/section, with Thomas Madden continuing as its Section Lead — direct continuity from the archived "Thomas S. Madden 1992 to present" entry.
programs.notes: The archived "Center for Creative Studies" = today's College for Creative Studies in Detroit (not the unrelated Sangamon-area or other "creative studies" entities). Archived faculty fully corroborated: Thomas P. Muir (1985–1991) preceded Thomas S. Madden, who is STILL listed on the live CCS faculty page as Professor / Section Lead of Metalsmithing and Jewelry — strong confirmation this is the same program. One search snippet states Madden was "Crafts Department Chairman 1992–2014"; he stepped down from the chair role around 2014 but remains a professor/section lead, so the program head role passed on while he stayed on faculty. programs.current_status: Active. Metals and Jewelry is one of the studio production fine-arts areas (alongside drawing, painting, sculpture, ceramics, printmaking, photography). It is a studio emphasis pursued within the BFA (Fine Arts Emphasis); the department also offers BA (Art History, Graphic Design, Licensure emphases), BFA Graphic Design/Licensure emphases, and a BSE in Art Education. programs.current_chair: Department chair not individually named on the public catalog page (dept contact: 262-472-1324, artanddesign@uww.edu). Current metals/jewelry professor is Teresa Faris.
programs.what_happened: Continuation with leadership succession. Linda Threadgill (the archived "to present" entry) headed the UW-Whitewater Metals Program from 1979 to 2003 and is now Professor Emerita (she now lives/works in Santa Fe, NM). The program continued under Teresa Faris, the current professor of metalsmithing and jewelry design. The area remains active through 2026 (recent UW System feature stories and a 2026 "International Recognition" UW-Whitewater news item cover the metals/jewelry program and its students). No closure, merger, or rename of the metals/jewelry offering was found; it remains a studio area within the Department of Art and Design.
programs.notes: Archived record listed Marcia Lewis (1973-1975) and Linda Threadgill ("? to present"). Threadgill's actual tenure heading the program was 1979-2003 per her Wikipedia bio; the directory's "to present" was already stale when archived. The metals/jewelry emphasis is not a standalone degree but a studio concentration within the BFA Fine Arts degree. Department chair name not surfaced on public pages; would require contacting the department. Confidence high that the program exists and is active; medium on the precise current chair identity (Teresa Faris confirmed as metals professor, not confirmed as dept chair).

The BFA in Art offers five concentrations: painting, photography, printmaking, sculpture, and time-based + media art. Metalworking survives as a shop facility (Walker Metal Shop, supporting metalsmithing/foundry/welding/blacksmithing) used by the Sculpture area, and as occasional non-degree jewelry-design workshops ("Fox Fridays"). The program sits in the College of Art within the Sam Fox School of Design & Visual Arts.
programs.current_chair: Meghan Kirkwood is Chair of Undergraduate Studio Art (College of Art). No dedicated metals/jewelry area head exists; the historic program was led by Heikki Seppä until his 1992 retirement.
programs.what_happened: The dedicated metalsmithing/silversmithing program was built by Heikki Seppä (faculty 1965–1992, with John Baltrusunas part-time 1972–1992). It did not survive Seppä's 1992 retirement as a distinct degree program; metals was absorbed into the broader Sculpture area and the metal shop. Seppä died May 18, 2010 (professor emeritus). By the 2014-onward period of the archived directory and today, there is no standalone metals/jewelry concentration — only the Sculpture concentration plus shared metal-shop facilities and short jewelry workshops. Current undergraduate studio leadership is Chair Meghan Kirkwood. This is a merge/dissolution of the named program rather than a closure of the school, which remains very active.
programs.notes: "Washington University" here = Washington University in St. Louis (confirmed by the Seppä/Baltrusunas faculty record). The historic standalone metals program no longer exists; metalsmithing is now subsumed under Sculpture within the College of Art (Sam Fox School, est. 2005 as the umbrella school). Could not find a named successor "metals area coordinator," consistent with the program no longer being a distinct track. Degree path for a student interested in metals today: BFA Art with a Sculpture concentration.

As of 2026 the Art Department remains active and continues to offer metalsmithing/jewelry as a studio discipline (jewelry studio + ART 2214 course), so the metals offering was a continuation, not a closure. No metals-specific closure was found; current art chair is Steven Pearson.
programs.notes: "Still exists" coded as merged-renamed because the SCHOOL was renamed (WMC -> McDaniel, 2002), while the metals/jewelry offering itself continued uninterrupted within the art department. programs.current_status: Institution renamed: Western Montana College became "University of Montana Western" in 2000. The standalone metals/jewelry/blacksmithing offering Brienza built no longer exists as a distinct program. Today there is a Department of Fine Arts offering a Bachelor of Arts in Visual Arts and a Bachelor of Arts in Glass (plus Associate degrees including "Visual Arts Craft" and "Associate of Arts: Glass," and Glass minor/certificate). No current jewelry/metalsmithing degree or concentration is listed; an ART 479 Advanced Studio - Artist Blacksmithing course still appears in the catalog. Glass became the surviving specialty (also founded by Brienza), now run by Ruth King.
programs.current_chair: Not findable. Current Fine Arts faculty include Ruth King (Associate Professor of Glass, manages the Glass program and Mary Baker Emerick Art Studio), Eva Mastandrea (Professor, visual arts/painting), and Stephen Alan Seder (Assistant Professor, theatre/media arts). No department chair is named on the public department page.
programs.what_happened: Renamed/absorbed into the Montana University System. The archived faculty record (Barney Brienza, 1971-present) is now historical: Brienza, who under his own initiative introduced and built the jewelry, stained glass, glass blowing, and artist-blacksmithing offerings (building many tools himself), retired around 2006-2007 after ~35-36 years. A retrospective exhibit honored his retirement at the Montana Western Art Gallery/Museum. After his departure the metals/jewelry teaching was not carried forward as a named program; the art unit consolidated as the Department of Fine Arts, with glass (Ruth King) emerging as the flagship studio specialty and broader Visual Arts BA/AA degrees. Since ~2014 the program has continued under this Fine Arts structure with no metals/jewelry degree.

Described by CWU as "the only dedicated four-year jewelry degree in Washington state."

programs.what_happened: Continuation, no closure or rename. The program has run continuously since the late 1950s through a lineage of internationally recognized professors (Ramona Solberg, Don Tompkins, Ken Cory, then Keith Lewis). Keith Lewis — listed in the archived record as "1993 to present" — remains the lead faculty member, now a CWU Distinguished Professor (inducted American Craft Council Fellow 2022; monograph presented at Munich Jewelry Week 2024; work at NYC Museum of Arts and Design 2024). The host department is now styled "Department of Art + Design." No closure, merger, or renaming of the metals program is evident; it remains an active BFA/MFA area.
programs.notes: Archived record matches reality: Solberg 1956–67, Cory 1972–94, Lewis 1993–present all corroborated (CWU cites the lineage Solberg → Tompkins → Cory → Lewis). The program is robustly active as of 2024–2026. Could not retrieve the precise catalog degree-code page (one program URL 404'd), but multiple CWU pages confirm BFA Studio Art (Jewelry & Metalsmithing) and a 90-credit MFA with a Jewelry & Metalsmithing concentration. The current department chair (administrative head of Art + Design) was not separately confirmed by name; Keith Lewis is the program's lead jewelry/metals professor.

programs.name: Florida Gulf Coast Art Center
programs.what_happened: Closed. The Florida Gulf Coast Art Center was a non-degree community art center in Belleair, FL (roots to the Belleair Arts Center, ~1936; long-running facility on land donated 1944, built 1948). It ran art classes/workshops and, in the 1980s, partnered with the Florida Society of Goldsmiths (FSG) on art-metal/jewelry workshops and the first exhibition of art-metal jewelry by Florida artists (May 1986). In 1999 the organization relocated to Pinewood Cultural Park in Largo, FL and was renamed the Gulf Coast Museum of Art. Facing severe financial pressure, the Gulf Coast Museum of Art closed in January 2009. Its permanent collection (contemporary Florida art) was transferred to St. Petersburg College (Florida International Museum), and the Largo building later became The Gallery at Creative Pinellas. The closure (2009) predates the directory's ~2014 offline window, so by the archived snapshot the program no longer existed.

Facilities (in the Fine/Eskenazi Fine Arts Building) were renovated, including CAD/CAM and 3D-modeling/computer-aided machining equipment.
programs.notes: Archived record (founded 1947; Eikerman 1947-1978; Long 1983-present) is corroborated. The program is still called "Metalsmithing + Jewelry Design." Note the parent-school rename: School of Fine Arts / Henry Radford Hope School of Fine Arts -> School of Art + Design -> Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design (named 2016). programs.current_status: Active. Jewelry/metalsmithing is one of eight media areas within the BFA in Art (formerly named Integrated Studio Arts) and the MFA in Integrated Visual Arts (63 credits). It sits in the Department of Art and Visual Culture, College of Design. Located in room 0044 of the College of Design building. Not a standalone degree — it is a concentration/studio area within the integrated studio art degrees.
programs.current_chair: Not confirmed from official pages (the AVC department site did not name the current chair; department contact anring@iastate.edu / (515) 294-0816). Joe Muench, professor of jewelry/metalsmithing (Chuck Evans's successor, ISU faculty 2001), retired in 2025; a current metals instructor was not confirmable.
programs.what_happened: Continuation with leadership succession, no closure. Chuck Evans (who founded/opened the ISU metals program, taught 1978-2001) retired in 2001 and died July 31, 2015 (age 75). His successor Joe Muench — a 1984 ISU craft-design graduate — joined the faculty in 2001 and taught metalsmithing/jewelry until retiring in 2025 (cited as health reasons). The program itself continues as an active studio area; the umbrella undergraduate degree was renamed from "Integrated Studio Arts" to "Art, BFA," and the graduate degree is the MFA in Integrated Visual Arts. A 2025 exhibition, "Lessons Learned: Explorations in Metal" at the Octagon Center for the Arts, marked Muench's legacy.
programs.notes: Do not confuse with the University of Iowa (Iowa City) Jewelry and Metal Arts program in its School of Art, Art History, and Design — a separate institution with its own dedicated BFA/MFA in Jewelry and Metal Arts. The archived record (Chuck Evans 1978-2001) matches Iowa State University (Ames), College of Design, where Evans opened the metals program. Current department chair and the post-2025 metals instructor could not be verified from the fetched official pages; recommend confirming via the AVC faculty directory.

programs.name: Maryland Institute College of Art (MICA) — Jewelry / Metalsmithing program (archived as "Maryland Art Institute, Jewelry Institute")
programs.current_name: Baltimore Jewelry Center (independent successor nonprofit); MICA itself no longer offers a jewelry/metals program
programs.current_status: As an academic degree program: CLOSED. MICA shut its Jewelry Center/Department in spring 2014 and offers no jewelry/metalsmithing major today (nearest current MICA programs are Interdisciplinary Sculpture and Fiber). The program's people, equipment, and mission continue OUTSIDE the college as the Baltimore Jewelry Center (BJC), an independent 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded in 2014. BJC offers non-degree, community/continuing education: 4-/6-/8-/12-week jewelry & metalsmithing classes, weekend workshops, online courses, kids/teens programs, and studio rental — not BFA/MFA degrees.
programs.current_chair: Baltimore Jewelry Center: Shane Prada was founding Executive Director (2014–2025); she announced her departure and BJC was recruiting a new Executive Director with an anticipated start ~October 2025 (successor name not yet confirmed in sources).
programs.what_happened: In late 2012 MICA judged its ~20-year-old Jewelry Department financially unsalvageable and closed the program in spring 2014. It was neither absorbed into nor renamed within MICA — the college dropped jewelry/metals entirely. In spring 2013 a core group of MICA jewelry faculty and students, led by Shane Prada, organized to preserve the program's legacy; in summer 2014 they launched the independent nonprofit Baltimore Jewelry Center (initially at Meadow Mill), negotiating donation of MICA's equipment. BJC has operated continuously since 2014 as a metalsmithing/art-jewelry education center. Leadership change ~2024–2025: founding director Shane Prada stepped down and BJC searched for a new Executive Director (start targeted Oct 2025).
programs.notes: "Maryland Art Institute, Jewelry Institute" in the archived directory is the Maryland Institute College of Art (MICA), Baltimore — specifically its Jewelry Center/Department. Harold O'Connor (metalsmith, b. 1941) was a visiting/workshop instructor, consistent with the "in 1982" archived note (he was a renowned itinerant goldsmithing-workshop teacher, not a permanent MICA faculty member). Important distinction: the academic program at MICA is permanently closed (still_exists "merged-renamed" is used here to capture that the program lives on, but as an independent community nonprofit rather than a degree-granting academic program; if classed strictly as "academic program survival" the answer is closed). No current degrees. Could not load baltimorejewelrycenter.org homepage directly (HTTP 403) but BJC offerings confirmed via cached fetch and secondary sources.

programs.current_name: Metalsmithing, School of Art and Design, Southern Illinois University Carbondale
programs.current_status: Active and thriving. Offers a BFA in Studio Art: Metalsmithing (120 cr) and an MFA in Art with two metals tracks: Blacksmithing and Small Metals (60 cr min). SIU bills itself as the only MFA blacksmithing program in the nation. The program sits in the School of Art and Design, within the College of Arts and Media (web-branded under "Art, Architecture, and Design"). The studios are in the historic Pulliam Industrial/Design wing (blacksmithing studio, plus jewelry/small-metals and casting spaces).
programs.current_chair: No single "metals program head" is published; the program is staffed by Rick (Richard E.) Smith, Professor — blacksmithing, and Sun Kyoung Kim, Associate Professor — small metals/jewelry. Smith effectively oversees the blacksmithing side. (Overall unit leadership = the School of Art and Design director, not specifically published on the metals page.)
programs.what_happened: Continuation with a generational faculty handoff. The program founded by L. Brent Kington (began rebuilding SIU metals after 1961; "reintroduced blacksmithing as an art form to the US"; Lifetime Achievement, SNAG 2011; the $1M endowed L. Brent Kington chair was created in 2006) and Richard Mawdsley (fine metals, from 1978) is now carried by Rick Smith (blacksmithing) and Sun Kyoung Kim (small metals/jewelry). Mawdsley and Kington are emeritus/deceased. Since ~2014 the program has continued uninterrupted, retaining both blacksmithing and small-metals/jewelry tracks at BFA and MFA levels; the academic unit has been reorganized/rebranded into the School of Art and Design under the College of Arts and Media.
programs.notes: The archived record's faculty (Kington 1961-1997, Hu 1968-69, Mawdsley 1978-present) all match the historical record; that "present" snapshot predates the current faculty. The directory's old institution name maps to today's SIU Carbondale "Metalsmithing" track. Did not find a formally titled "metals program coordinator." Confidence high on existence/degrees/faculty; medium on exact internal leadership title.
